summary: This unit teaches you to develop partnering arrangements between a public body and other organisations such as NGOs, community groups, universities and private firms. You will learn when partnering is the right choice, how to define goals, choose partners fairly and carry out due diligence, how to share contributions and risks, and what a partnering agreement must contain. You will also learn how to govern the partnership, build trust, monitor results, handle problems, stay accountable for public money and end or renew the arrangement.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. Many public problems, such as youth unemployment, school nutrition, community health and urban markets, are too big for one ministry or corporation to solve alone. A **partnering arrangement** is an agreement in which a public body works with one or more other organisations towards a shared goal, each contributing something the others lack. This unit shows you how to develop such arrangements so that they are fair, lawful, good value for public money and likely to last.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in a public body
rows: Define the problem and goals, compare partnering with doing it alone or buying a service, and choose the right type of arrangement.
Set clear, measurable shared objectives and identify who needs to be involved.
Set criteria and weights, score proposals, carry out due diligence, declare conflicts and follow procurement rules.
Work out cash and in-kind shares, match funding and value for money.
Cover purpose, roles, governance, risks, reporting, data, communications, disputes, change and exit; get legal review and proper authority.
Create governance, trust and fair treatment, especially for small community partners.
Require reports and checks on public money passed to partners.
Track targets, handle problems, plan sustainability, decide on renewal and record lessons.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenarios and sums (weighted scores, cost shares, in-kind values, percentages).
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and sums) and longer answers on planning a partnership, comparing types of agreement, drafting, risk and handling problems.
**Practical group tasks**: scoping a partnership and recommending a partner from three proposals; and negotiating and drafting a partnering agreement in a role play.

blocks.note: Short-answer questions ask for exact terms: in-kind contribution, letter of intent, value for money, joint venture, steering committee, mediation, synergy, accountability, match funding, beneficiaries, force majeure and term. Learn them from the key terms in the Revision section.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: What partnering is, and when to use it

blocks.p: A partnership makes sense when **each side brings something the other lacks, towards a shared goal**. For example, a ministry wants to expand after-school reading classes in a rural parish. A church network or a community group may already have buildings, volunteers and the community's trust. The ministry may have funds, trained teachers and materials. Together they reach more children, at lower cost, than either could alone.

head: Benefit
Example
rows: An NGO that knows local youth works with a ministry that has training funds
A firm gives equipment or premises; a ministry gives funding and staff
A community group helps the agency reach residents who do not trust offices
Shared cost; services delivered at lower unit cost
Partners together achieve **more than they could separately**

ul: When the task is a **legal duty that only the public body itself may perform** (for example, a decision a law gives to a named officer).
When the partner has an interest that conflicts with the public purpose.
When no partner has what is needed, or the cost of managing the partnership is more than the benefit.
When the goal can be reached more simply by buying a service under a contract.

blocks.p: Partnerships range from loose to tight. Choose the level of closeness that the goal needs. More closeness gives more shared results, but needs more trust, time and formal agreement.

head: Level
What it means
Example
rows: Two agencies share news of their programmes
Adjusting activities to avoid overlap, but planning and funding separately
Two agencies agree different days for mobile clinics in the same parish
Helping each other with resources or referrals
A ministry lends a hall for an NGO's class
Planning and delivering a joint programme with shared goals and some shared funding
A ministry and an NGO run one youth skills course together
Merging functions or creating a shared body
A joint venture or shared service

head: Arrangement
What it is
When it fits
rows: A short document recording that the parties **intend** to make an agreement, before the full agreement is drafted
Early stage, to show commitment and agree how talks will proceed
A document recording shared aims and how the parties will cooperate; usually **not legally binding** for money obligations
Two agencies, or an agency and an NGO, working together without large payments
A **binding** agreement. When a public body pays a private firm to deliver a service to agreed standards, a contract awarded under the **procurement rules** is normally needed
Buying goods or services; passing significant public funds with clear duties
A document that sets out a service one agency provides to another, for a fee or not, with turnaround times and quality standards
One agency provides payroll processing for another
A **long-term** deal in which a private firm shares a public project's risks, often by building, financing and operating an asset
A market, a road, a facility, run for many years
A new business entity owned jointly by two or more partners for a specific purpose
Partners create a company to run a facility

blocks.note: The right form depends on the money, the risk, the legal duties and the time. An MoU cannot replace a contract where public funds are at risk. Take legal advice before you choose.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: The Government of Jamaica has a public-private partnership policy and agencies that support such projects. Large partnerships involve cabinet or ministry approvals and special procedures. This unit gives the general principles; your ministry's legal unit and finance unit say which procedures apply.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Value for money** means getting the best mix of cost, quality and results from public funds. It is not the same as the lowest price. If a ministry can deliver a training programme itself for J$24,000,000 or through a partnership that costs it J$18,000,000 for the same results, the partnership **may** give better value, **if the risks are managed**. Compare costs per result and include management time and risk.

**Worked example.** A partnership costs the ministry J$36,000,000 and trains 1,800 people: 36,000,000 ÷ 1,800 = **J$20,000** per person. Doing it alone would cost J$24,000 per person. The ministry saves J$4,000 per person, or J$7,200,000 over 1,800 people. Then ask whether quality and results were as good.

sections.title: Scoping the partnership and choosing partners

blocks.h: Step 1: define the problem, goals and needs

blocks.p: Before looking for partners, a parish municipal corporation or ministry should **define the problem, the goals and what it needs from a partner**. A partner chosen before the need is clear will shape the project around its own interests.

flow: **Define the problem** with evidence: who is affected, how many, where
**Set the goal** and make it SMART
**Decide what you need**: money, skills, premises, reach, trust, technology
**Check your own legal powers and rules**, and whether partnering is allowed
**Identify stakeholders**: who will be affected or can help (residents, schools, firms, NGOs, other agencies)
**Set an outline budget** and the contribution you can make
**Get approval** to go ahead from the person who holds the authority

blocks.p: A shared objective is specific, measurable, agreed by all partners and has a date. Compare:

head: Weak
Strong
rows: "Screen 2,500 adults in Clarendon for diabetes by 31 March 2027, with 90% of those found at risk referred to a clinic"
"Train 600 young people aged 17 to 24 in three western parishes in basic electrical wiring, with 300 placed in work or apprenticeships within six months"
"Provide a breakfast five days a week to 1,200 pupils at 12 named schools during the 2026-27 school year"

ul: Use an **open, fair process**: advertise a call for proposals or an expression of interest where the law or policy requires it.
Publish the **criteria** in advance. Clear, published criteria make the choice **fair, open and able to be justified** if challenged.
Follow the **procurement rules** where the arrangement is, in substance, buying goods or services.
Do not give any organisation an unfair advantage or inside information.

blocks.p: Set the criteria and weights **before** the proposals are opened. Score each proposal on each criterion, multiply by the weight and add up. Weights total 100%.
**Worked example.** Criteria and weights: capacity 45%, community links 30%, cost 25%. Scores are out of 10, and a high cost score means good value.

Y has the highest score. The score guides the decision; it does not replace the due diligence, references, interviews and judgement that also go into the recommendation. Record why the choice was made.

**Due diligence** is the careful checking of a possible partner **before** any commitment. Its purpose is to check the partner's **legal status, finances, record and capacity**, and that nothing in its background would harm the public body.

head: Area
What to check
rows: Registration, who the directors or officers are, authority to sign, tax compliance and any required licences
Audited accounts, annual returns filed, sources of income, debts, ability to carry the project cash flow
Past projects, references, evaluation reports, complaints, any legal disputes
Staff, skills, premises, equipment, systems for reporting and safeguarding
Conflicts of interest, links to staff of your body, reputation, insurance
Policies for working with children and vulnerable people; how data is protected

blocks.p: If due diligence finds a problem, such as annual returns not filed or accounts not audited for years, **raise it with the partner, weigh the risk, and decide**: ask for it to be put right, add safeguards (for example payment in stages) or choose another partner. Do not ignore it.

An officer who helps to choose a partner and is a director of one of the bidding organisations, or whose close relative is, must **declare the interest in writing and take no part** in the decision. Another officer decides. Record this.

blocks.note: Do not accept gifts, hospitality or offers from organisations that want to partner with you while a decision is open. Follow your body's gift and conflict of interest policy.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Type
Meaning
Example
rows: Staff time, premises or equipment given **instead of cash**
An NGO provides four staff for six months; a church gives a hall
Each partner puts in money in an **agreed ratio**
A donor gives J$1 for every J$2 the agency puts in
A university designs the training course
A community group introduces staff to residents

blocks.p: **Worked example: cost shares.** A project costs J$30,000,000. The agency pays 50%, a private firm 30% and an NGO 20%.
**Worked example: in-kind value.** An NGO provides 3 staff for 4 months, each valued at J$120,000 a month, and a hall at J$80,000 a month for 4 months.

**Worked example: match funding.** A donor will give J$1 for every J$2 of agency money. If the agency puts in J$8,000,000, the donor gives 8,000,000 ÷ 2 = **J$4,000,000**, and the total is J$12,000,000.

blocks.note: Agree in writing how in-kind contributions will be valued and recorded, so that each partner's share can be checked and no one is accused of under-contributing.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Every project has risks: money, delay, quality, safety, reputation, changes in law, bad weather. The principle is that **each risk goes to the partner best able to manage it**. For example, in a partnership to build and run a market:

head: Risk
Best placed with
rows: Shared, depending on who markets the stalls
Insurance, and the partner that controls the asset
The partner that operates the facility, with oversight by the corporation

blocks.p: Write the allocation into the agreement and keep a **risk register**: each risk, who owns it, what is being done and how it will be checked.

ul: Free offers can carry hidden costs: management time, branding obligations, exclusivity or limits on policy.
A private firm that offers to fund a school nutrition programme if its sugary drink brand appears on all the materials creates a clash with the programme's **health aims**. Decline or negotiate.
A partner who asks for **exclusive rights to all future projects** in a parish limits fair competition and value for money. Decline.

blocks.p: A written agreement turns good intentions into clear commitments. It protects the public body, the partners and the public. **Legal officers review it** before a director signs, and the person who signs must have **written authority** for that amount. An officer whose written authority lets her sign up to J$2,000,000 may not sign a J$15,000,000 co-funding agreement: she must **refer it to the officer who has authority for that amount**.

head: Section
What it says
Why it is needed
rows: The agreed length of time the agreement lasts
So tasks are not missed or doubled, and each can be held to account
Cash, in-kind, dates, conditions and how they are valued
Prevents disputes over who gives what
Who decides what, how, and how often the partners meet
Risks are managed by the right partner
Reports, dates, financial records, rights of access and audit
Who owns materials or software and who may use them; how personal data is protected
How messages, branding and credit are agreed
Changes only in writing, agreed by the partners
Steps in order: talks, senior officers, mediation, then other remedies
A clause that excuses duties when events beyond control, such as a hurricane, stop the work
How and when partners may leave, notice, what happens to assets, records and unfinished work
How benefits will last after funding ends

blocks.note: An agreement should not include irrelevant items such as the home addresses of staff. Include only what the partners need to know, and keep personal data to the minimum.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: If a university and a ministry will jointly develop a training app for farmers, the agreement should say **who owns it, who may use it and how farmers' data is protected**. If two agencies share records of the clients they both serve, the agreement should say what data is shared, why, and how it is kept secure, in line with the general purpose of the data protection law.

flow: The partnership managers try to settle the problem between them
If they cannot, it goes to the partners' **senior officers**, who meet to settle it (for example a disagreement about sharing a cost overrun)
If still unresolved, **mediation**: a neutral third person helps the partners to reach their own agreement
Only then other legal remedies, as the agreement and the law allow

blocks.p: If both partners want to change delivery dates, they should **agree the change in writing, as the agreement allows**, signed by the persons with authority. Verbal changes are easily disputed and may breach funding rules.

ul: Prepare for a negotiation: know your aims, your limits, the other side's likely interests and what you can trade.
Look for **shared interests**, not just positions.
Be firm on principles of fairness, law and public value; be flexible on details.
Record agreed points at each stage; do not sign until the legal review and authority are complete.

head: Body or role
Job
rows: The group of senior people from each partner that oversees the partnership and makes its **key decisions**: budget changes, direction, resolving disputes
Appointed by each partner; the **daily contact**, who keeps the joint work on track, handles issues and reports to the steering committee
Teams that handle particular tasks, such as training, finance or communications
Residents and users who advise on the design and delivery

blocks.p: Governance should say **who decides what, how, and how often the partners meet**.

ul: **Share information openly** and do what you promised: the practices that do most to build trust early.
Meet regularly, and listen.
Admit problems early.
Give credit fairly to every partner.

Agree realistic timelines, and explain your own approval steps early. A private firm that decides quickly and a ministry that needs several approvals will clash unless both understand the other's timetable.

blocks.p: When a large ministry partners with a small community group, for example in a Kingston inner-city community, there is a risk that the larger partner dominates. To make the partnership work well:

ul: **Respect the group's knowledge** and give it a **real say** in design and decisions.
Agree **reporting requirements** that are proportionate: a small group cannot produce the paperwork of a large agency.
Pay on time; late payment can threaten a small group's survival.
Offer **capacity building** (training in financial reporting, for example).
Do not make the group depend on a single funding source with no plan for the future.

blocks.p: A parish council that develops a partnership to manage a community park should **involve local residents** from the start. Residents can shape the plans and help the park succeed, and will take more care of a facility they helped to design.

When a ministry passes J$5,000,000 to a partner NGO, **the ministry remains accountable** for showing how the public money was used. Accountability means being answerable for how public money and decisions are used. Controls to include:

ul: Payments **in stages**, tied to milestones and reports;
a separate project **bank account** or clear accounting records;
regular **financial and progress reports** with evidence;
the right to **inspect records and audit**;
**spot checks** and site visits;
rules on **procurement** by the partner when spending public money;
repayment of unspent or misused funds;
a clause for ending the agreement if the funds are misused.

blocks.note: A partner organisation that receives public funds is expected to be open about how it spends them. Do not accept a partner that refuses audit or reporting.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Agree **measures and targets at the start**, and review them together. Two kinds of measure are needed.

head: Kind
What it measures
Examples
rows: Households reached; people trained; clinic visits; savings; satisfaction
How well partners communicate, trust and work together
Meeting attendance; time to answer requests; partner feedback; conflicts raised

blocks.p: **Worked example.** A partner has reached 840 households against a target of 1,200. 840 ÷ 1,200 × 100 = **70%** of the target.

If a partner's quarterly report shows it is behind on its agreed targets, the agency's partnership manager should **meet the partner first, to find the causes and agree a recovery plan**, rather than jump to penalties.

flow: Check the figures and the reports
Meet the partner: ask what is causing the delay (resources, weather, staff, data, unrealistic targets)
Agree a **recovery plan** with actions, owners and dates
Support where possible, for example training or unblocking an approval
Monitor closely and report to the steering committee
If there is no progress, follow the agreement's dispute and remedies steps

blocks.p: Six months in, if a partner is behind its targets, reports are late and meetings are tense, the partnership manager should deal with both the work and the relationship: meet privately to listen; acknowledge pressures; clarify roles and expectations; set up fewer, clearer meetings; agree communication rules; use the steering committee if needed; and consider mediation. A partnership "health check" looks beyond results at how partners communicate, trust and work together.

Partners should report their joint achievements to stakeholders, giving **fair credit to each partner**. It builds goodwill, supports funding and keeps partners committed. Agree the message in advance under the communications protocol.

A donor-funded partnership will end in two years. Partners should **plan now how the work will be funded and run after the donor leaves**: other funding sources, a share of costs by the partners, training local staff, handing over assets, and fitting the work into regular budgets.

flow: Before the agreement ends, partners **review results, costs and the relationship** against the original aims
Compare cost per result with what an alternative would cost (value for money)
Consult beneficiaries and stakeholders
Decide: **renew, change, or end**; agree this in writing
If ending, follow the **exit section**: close accounts, settle assets, transfer records and tell stakeholders
Hold a **lessons-learned** review so future partnerships avoid problems and repeat successes

blocks.p: **Worked example.** A three-year training partnership cost J$45,000,000 and trained 2,400 people against a target of 3,000. Results: 2,400 ÷ 3,000 × 100 = 80% of target. Cost per person: 45,000,000 ÷ 2,400 = J$18,750. If the agency's own cost is J$22,000 per person, the partnership gives better value per person. A renewal decision would also look at quality, reach and risks.

blocks.note: Record lessons at the end of every partnership: what worked, what did not, what you would change. Share them with colleagues, so the next team does not repeat the same mistakes.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: explain why a public body partners, and when partnering is not suitable.

c1.title: Choosing a youth training partner in Westmoreland
c1.text: A parish municipal corporation in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, wants a partner to run a skills programme for young people. It published criteria and weights before opening proposals: capacity 45%, community links 30% and cost 25% (a high cost score means good value). Organisation X scores 7, 9 and 6. Organisation Y scores 9, 6 and 8. Organisation Z scores 8, 7 and 5. Due diligence shows that Y's accounts were last audited four years ago. A member of the evaluation team, Mr Samuels, is a director of Organisation Z.

c2.title: Refurbishing a community centre in Old Harbour
c2.text: A community centre in Old Harbour, St Catherine, will be refurbished at a total cost of J$30,000,000. The agency will pay 50%, a private firm 30% and an NGO 20%. The NGO will meet part of its share by providing 3 staff for 4 months, each valued at J$120,000 a month, and the hall at J$80,000 a month for the 4 months. The firm will provide materials at its own cost. The firm wants to start work on site next week, relying on a letter of intent, before the co-funding agreement is signed.

c3.title: A school breakfast programme in St Thomas and Portland
c3.text: A ministry and a private company have agreed in principle to run a school breakfast scheme for 1,200 pupils in 12 schools in St Thomas and Portland. They are now drafting the agreement. The company wants to put its logo on all materials and to review all media statements before they are issued. It also wants the right to take photographs of pupils for its own advertising. A hurricane in the area last year closed several schools for three weeks. The ministry's legal officers have not yet seen the draft.

c4.title: A partnership with a community group in Denham Town
c4.text: A large government agency wants to work with a small community-based organisation in Denham Town, Kingston, to run a homework centre for 150 children. The organisation has run activities for the community for ten years and is trusted by residents. It has three part-time staff and little experience of formal reporting. The agency's first draft requires monthly financial reports in the agency's own format and pays its grant in one amount at the end of the year. The agency's staff have decided the programme design without meeting the group.

c5.title: A training partnership that is falling behind
c5.text: A ministry gave J$12,000,000 to an NGO under a one-year partnership to train 1,500 young people. After six months, the NGO has trained 480 people against a half-year target of 750, its quarterly report is three weeks late, and meetings with the ministry's partnership manager have become tense. The NGO says that its trainers lost three weeks after a storm. The ministry's own training costs J$9,000 per person.

questions.q: Using the published weights, which organisation has the highest weighted score?
o: X, with 7.35
Z, with 6.95
Y, with 7.85
Z, with 7.65

questions.q: The accounts of Organisation Y were last audited four years ago. What should the corporation do?
o: Raise it with Y and weigh the risk, then ask for audited accounts or add safeguards
Ignore it, since Y has the highest score and the published criteria did not mention audits
Reject Y at once without discussion, because an audit gap is always a disqualifying fault
Choose X instead and tell Y that its proposal scored lower on cost
questions.why: Due diligence findings must be weighed, not ignored. The corporation should ask Y for an explanation, require audited accounts or add safeguards such as staged payments, then decide.

questions.q: Mr Samuels is a director of Organisation Z. What must happen?
o: He scores only Organisation Z and leaves the others to his colleagues
He continues in the team, but another officer checks his scoring of Z
He tells the team verbally and then votes on every proposal as before
He declares the interest in writing and takes no part in scoring or deciding
questions.why: A conflict of interest must be declared, ideally in writing, and the officer must take no part in the evaluation or decision. The declaration is recorded.

questions.q: Why did the corporation publish the criteria and weights before opening the proposals?
o: So that organisations can adjust their proposals to score the maximum points
So that the choice is fair and open and can be justified if challenged
So that the evaluation team does not need to write a report on its decision
So that the corporation can change the weights if it prefers another winner
questions.why: Setting criteria in advance prevents the choice from being shaped to suit a preferred bidder, and gives a clear basis for the decision.

questions.q: What is the NGO's total share of the cost, in cash and in-kind together?
questions.why: 20% of J$30,000,000 = J$6,000,000. The agency pays J$15,000,000 (50%) and the firm J$9,000,000 (30%). J$1,760,000 is only the NGO's in-kind part.

questions.q: The NGO's in-kind contribution (3 staff for 4 months at J$120,000 each a month, plus the hall) is J$1,760,000. How much of its share must it still pay in cash?
questions.why: J$6,000,000 minus J$1,760,000 = J$4,240,000. (J$4,560,000 leaves out the J$320,000 value of the hall.)

questions.q: The firm wants to begin site work next week, relying only on the letter of intent. What is the main risk?
o: Without a signed agreement, duties, payments and risks are not fixed or binding
The letter of intent expires one week after it is issued by either party
The firm would need the NGO's permission before starting any work
Site work can start only after the legal officers have inspected the site
questions.why: A letter of intent records an intention to agree. Until the full agreement is signed, the partners' duties, payments and risk allocation are not settled.

questions.q: What should the agency do to make sure the in-kind contributions can be checked later?
o: Accept the NGO's own estimates and make no record of them
Count only the cash contributions and ignore in-kind help in the report
Agree in the agreement how they will be valued and recorded
Ask the NGO to invoice the agency for its staff costs at the end
questions.why: A written agreement on valuation and records lets each partner's share be checked and avoids disputes.

questions.q: The company wants to review all media statements before they are issued. What is the best way to deal with this?
o: Agree, since the company is paying part of the cost and so its views matter most to the ministry
Refuse, since a public body must never consult a partner about any of its public statements
Leave the matter out of the agreement and settle each case as it arises in the programme
Agree a communications protocol on who approves messages, branding and credit
questions.why: A communications protocol makes messages consistent and gives each partner fair credit, without giving one partner a veto over public information.

questions.q: The company wants to photograph pupils for its own advertising. What is the main concern?
o: The company will have to pay each pupil's family for the use of the photograph
Children's images need parental consent and data protection, so the use must be limited
The pupils may be late for their first class if the photographs are being taken
Photographs of pupils can be taken only by the ministry's official photographer
questions.why: Children's images and personal data need parental consent and protection. The agreement should say what may be used, by whom and for what purpose.

questions.q: Which clause best deals with the risk of another hurricane closing schools?
o: A clause making the ministry pay for all of the costs that are caused by any school closure
A clause that ends the agreement automatically if schools close for any length of time
A force majeure clause covering duties and payments when events beyond control stop the work
No clause is needed, because hurricanes are covered by the company's general insurance
questions.why: Force majeure excuses duties fairly when events beyond the partners' control, such as a hurricane, stop the work, and says how the project resumes.

questions.q: What should happen before the ministry's director signs the draft?
o: The ministry's legal officers review it and the necessary approvals are obtained
The company's lawyers review it, because they have drafted most of the text of it
The partners sign first and the legal officers review it within the next month
The principal of each of the schools reads it and gives written consent to it
questions.why: A partnering agreement is a legal document. Legal review and written approval from the right authority come before signing.

questions.q: The agency's draft requires monthly reports in its own format and pays the grant in one amount at the end of the year. What is the main problem?
o: The group may not cope with the reporting, and late payment could threaten its survival
The agency will have no real way to check how the money has been spent during the year
The reports will take the agency's own staff too long to read and check each month
The group will have no incentive to deliver the programme to the agency's standard
questions.why: Proportionate reporting and timely payment, perhaps in stages, are essential for small partners. Capacity building can also help.

questions.q: The agency's staff have already decided the programme design. What should the agency do?
o: Show the design to the group and ask for comments in the next week
Keep the design and add the group's name to the front page
Meet the group and give it a real say in design, using its knowledge
Wait until the first month's results before asking the group's views
questions.why: The group knows the community and has its trust. Respecting its knowledge and giving it a real say makes the programme more likely to succeed.

questions.q: Which step would best help the agency to hold the group accountable without overburdening it?
o: Require a full audit by an outside firm every month, at the group's own cost
Pay in stages tied to simple milestones, with short reports and occasional visits
Pay nothing until the whole programme has been fully delivered to the agency
Rely on the group's word, since it is trusted, and make no checks at all
questions.why: Staged payments with proportionate reporting and visits give control without breaking a small group. Monthly audits or no checks would each fail.

questions.q: Which clause will best help the homework centre to last after the grant ends?
o: A clause that makes the agency the owner of all of the centre's equipment and materials
A clause that ends the agreement as soon as the whole grant has been paid
A clause that allows the agency to change the programme at any time it chooses
A sustainability plan on future funding, staff training and who runs the centre
questions.why: Planning from the start how the work will be funded and run after the grant ends is the best way to make benefits last.

questions.q: What percentage of its half-year target has the NGO reached?
questions.why: 480 ÷ 750 × 100 = 64%. (32% would be 480 ÷ 1,500, the full-year target.)

questions.q: What should the partnership manager do first?
o: Meet the NGO to find the causes and agree a recovery plan
Stop all payments until the NGO catches up with the half-year target
Report the NGO to the steering committee as having broken the agreement
Find another organisation to take over the training programme
questions.why: Start with the causes, which may be outside the NGO's control, such as the storm, and agree a recovery plan with actions and dates.

questions.q: The NGO's quarterly report is three weeks late. How is the ministry's accountability affected?
o: The ministry is no longer accountable, since the NGO now holds all of the money
The NGO is accountable only to its own board of directors, not to the ministry
The ministry is accountable only for the part of the money it has not yet paid out
The ministry remains accountable for the J$12,000,000 and must require reports
questions.why: Passing money to a partner does not pass the duty to account for it. The ministry must require reports and check how the funds are used.

questions.q: If the NGO trains all 1,500 young people for the J$12,000,000, what is the cost per person, and how does it compare with the ministry's own cost?
o: J$16,000, found by dividing by the half-year target, so that it is poor value for money
J$25,000, found by dividing by the 480 people trained so far, so it is poor value
J$8,000, below the ministry's J$9,000, so it may be better value if the target is met
J$8,000, but a partnership's cost can never be compared with the ministry's own cost
questions.why: 12,000,000 ÷ 1,500 = J$8,000 per person, which is less than J$9,000. Value for money also depends on quality and on reaching the target, so the ministry should keep monitoring.
